patient.chief_complaint: Five-day progressive dysphagia and arm weakness with nasal speech, no preceding infection recalled, gait preserved.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. D. is a 32-year-old graphic designer presenting with a 5-day history of progressive oropharyngeal and upper extremity weakness. He initially noticed mild difficulty swallowing solid food approximately 5 days ago, which has progressed to coughing on thin liquids. Two days ago, he developed bilateral arm weakness making it difficult to lift objects overhead or type at his workstation. He recalls a low-grade fever with mild malaise approximately 10 days prior that he attributed to fatigue and resolved spontaneously without medical attention. He denies any bloody diarrhea or respiratory illness. He has no diplopia, no ptosis, and no lower extremity weakness — notably, he was able to walk into the emergency department unassisted and his gait appears normal. His speech has a nasal quality and he cannot clear his throat effectively. He has no sensory deficits. His partner noted that he had been having trouble buttoning his shirt for the past 3 days. He denies any prior neurological symptoms, and there is no family history of neuromuscular disease. There is no honey exposure, no wound, no tick exposure, and no canned food ingestion that would suggest botulism. The descending pattern with predominant bulbar and arm involvement — with preserved leg strength and absent upper extremity reflexes — is an atypical distribution.

differential.key_features: Bulbar weakness and arm weakness possible in MG, but reflexes preserved and fatigability pattern; AChR or MuSK antibodies and RNS / single-fibre EMG distinguish.
Descending bulbar + cervical pattern fits; but sensory symptoms or paresthesias are not classic for botulism; food / wound history negative.
Symmetric bilateral pattern with no crossed signs and preserved consciousness argues against brainstem stroke; MRI excludes.
Pharyngeal involvement possible; vaccination status and pharyngeal exam, plus rarity in vaccinated populations, make this unlikely.
Trismus and rigidity rather than weakness with areflexia.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, HIV, anti-GM1/anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies, and stool culture / Campylobacter serology if recent diarrhea
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis / elevated inflammatory markers reflecting antecedent infection; ganglioside antibodies for variant typing; trigger identification (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV)

optimal_actions.action: Order nerve conduction studies and needle EMG (EMG/NCS)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating pattern (prolonged DML, conduction block, reduced CV, absent F-waves) consistent with AIDP, or reduced CMAP amplitudes in axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with cell count <10/μL; may be normal in the first week of illness

optimal_actions.action: Order bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) and repeat every 4–6 hours
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline and serial FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF; deterioration to FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP worse than -30 cmH2O, or VC <40% predicted triggers ICU transfer / intubation

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for IVIG vs plasma exchange evidence to guide disease-modifying therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) and plasma exchange are equivalently effective first-line therapies; combination not superior

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions / contraindications for IVIG (renal function, IgA deficiency screen) and/or plasma exchange (coagulation, calcium, hemodynamics)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirmation that IVIG can be given safely (no severe renal impairment, no IgA deficiency) or that plasma exchange is appropriate (adequate vascular access, stable coagulation)

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia; conduction or repolarisation abnormalities reflecting autonomic involvement

optimal_actions.action: Initiate continuous cardiac telemetry for the first 1–2 weeks for moderate/severe disease — autonomic instability (bradyarrhythmias, BP lability) is common
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Documentation of sinus pauses, bradyarrhythmias, BP lability, or non-sustained tachyarrhythmias

useless_tools.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

critical_actions: Admit to a monitored unit given bulbar and respiratory risk.
Initiate IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (PLEX alternative).
Send anti-GT1a / anti-GQ1b IgG; CMV serology and PCR.
Nil per os until safe swallow confirmed; speech / swallow consult.
contraindicated_actions: Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
Do not assume MG without serological confirmation if RNS or single-fibre EMG is unavailable.
key_reasoning_points: PCB variant of GBS presents with bulbar, cervical, and proximal upper-limb weakness, often without leg involvement at onset.
Anti-GT1a (and sometimes anti-GQ1b) IgG is the serological marker.
Bulbar dysphagia and respiratory monitoring drive disposition decisions even when limb strength is relatively preserved.
Brainstem MRI is appropriate in this presentation to exclude brainstem stroke given the cranial-nerve predominance.

red_herrings.data_point: Absence of leg weakness with bulbar predominance
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest myasthenia gravis or brainstem disease rather than a regional GBS variant.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant of GBS classically spares legs; areflexia plus albuminocytologic dissociation place the diagnosis squarely within the GBS spectrum.

metadata.difficulty_description: Atypical PCB variant with descending pattern and leg sparing — requires recognizing GBS without classic ascending paralysis
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required tools, 1 red herring(s); classic or near-classic GBS workup with one or more plausible mimics that need active exclusion.
case_body_concerns: Bedside respiratory function (FVC/MIP/MEP/NIF) is delivered via an `interpret_labs` followup panel rather than `order_specialized_test{test_type=respiratory_function}` as the criteria pack mandates. Agents calling order_specialized_test{respiratory_function} will hit the EMG/NCS output instead.
